title: QUIC RFC 9000 Peer Connection-ID Lifecycle Runtime Architecture
purpose: Describe the bounded runtime path that tracks peer-issued connection IDs, applies Retire Prior To cleanup, emits required RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames, and enforces active connection-ID limits without claiming broad migration routing support.
design_summary: The peer connection-ID state keeps a sequence-indexed active set plus a historical reverse lookup so retired or duplicate values cannot be reintroduced under a different sequence. The runtime treats the handshake destination connection ID as implicit peer sequence 0 when processing NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames, removes all active entries below an increased Retire Prior To value before adding the new entry, and emits RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames for the removed sequences. After retire/add processing, the runtime closes with CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR if the peer-provided active set would exceed the local active_connection_id_limit. Local connection-ID issuance also observes the peer's active_connection_id_limit by rejecting an additional issued ID when the implicit initial ID plus already-issued active IDs would exceed the peer's limit.
data_and_state_considerations: The active set is runtime-local connection state. Connection ID bytes are copied before storage, stateless reset tokens remain copied for later comparison, and retired values remain reserved in the historical reverse lookup to preserve no-reuse validation. Retire Prior To cleanup updates outbound destination selection to the highest remaining sequence and queues retirement frames on the existing protected application-data send path.
edge_cases_and_constraints: A peer that requires zero-length destination connection IDs cannot later supply NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames.
Retire Prior To values greater than the frame sequence number remain protocol violations.
An exact duplicate NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame is accepted without increasing the active set.
Retire Prior To is applied before active-limit enforcement so temporary excess is only allowed when the frame also retires enough lower sequences.
The slice does not change route registration, public migration APIs, preferred-address transition behavior, or interop-runner migration success classification.
alternatives_considered: Treat the broad RFC 9000 transport artifact as sufficient; rejected because this state-machine proof needed direct requirement-home evidence and a narrower out-of-scope boundary.
Combine this with full migration and preferred-address routing; rejected because S9P5/S9P6 remain separate path-management proof clusters.
Retire old connection IDs after adding the new connection ID; rejected because RFC 9000 requires Retire Prior To cleanup before active-set limit evaluation.
risks: The current selection policy still uses the highest active peer-issued sequence for outbound destination connection IDs.
RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID emission is best-effort on the existing protected application-data send path and depends on ordinary send boundary checks.
This proof can be overstated as full migration support if kept out of its bounded peer-CID lifecycle context.

supplemental_sections.heading: Scope
supplemental_sections.content: This design covers only peer-issued connection-ID set maintenance, Retire Prior To cleanup, local and peer active connection-ID limit enforcement, and protected RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID emission for retired peer-issued sequences. It does not claim S9P5 migration discipline, S9P6 preferred-address transition, endpoint route registration for newly issued local connection IDs, public migration controls, multipath behavior, or interop migration success.
